titre: The Sign Language of Martha's Vineyard, Revisited
accroche: The whole island signed, says the classic account, going back to 17th-century English settlers. A 2024 study moves the origin forward by nearly a century.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the American island of Martha's Vineyard, off Massachusetts, deaf and hearing people talk to each other in sign language without anyone seeing it as a matter of assistance: everyone knows it, because everyone has a deaf neighbor or relative. That is the image fixed in 1985 by the anthropologist Nora Ellen Groce in her book *Everyone Here Spoke Sign Language*, which became the standard reference on the subject. She tied the signing community to settlers from Kent, England, carrying a recessive gene for deafness, and gave it an origin of 1692: the community would thus have enjoyed 133 years of independent development, until 1825.

## A Genealogy Redone from the Start

In 2024, the linguists Justin Power and Richard Meier republished the case file in the *Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education*, working from demographic and genealogical sources: they identified 53 deaf people who lived on the island between 1692 and 1998. Their conclusion moves the starting point: the Chilmark signing community, in their view, was born not in 1692 but in February 1785, 93 years later, with the birth of Benjamin Mayhew, son of Benjamin and Lydia Mayhew. Nine deaf people had lived on the island before him, but none in Chilmark in 1785: Lydia, married in 1784, said she had never seen a person in that condition before encountering one at a funeral in late 1784, when she was pregnant with Benjamin. The authors judge this account probably accurate.

They then separate two stories that the classic account blended. The recessive gene for deafness, which Groce brings from Kent, belongs to the island's population; the signing community, for its part, would be new, with no connection to earlier signing communities in Kent.

## Forty Years, Not 133

On October 25, 1825, three young deaf women from the island, Lovey Mayhew, Sally Smith, and Mary Smith, entered the American School for the Deaf in Hartford, which had opened in April 1817, eight years earlier. From 1785 to 1825 is about 40 years: the time, according to the authors, during which a signing community of the island's own could develop, before its encounter with the one at Hartford. The isolation was not complete (Rebecca Tilton knew the Mayhews and the Smiths before the birth of her first deaf child in 1818) but it was, in their view, a brief period of independent development.

The figures change too. Groce counted at least 72 deaf people and a peak of 45 in the 1840s; Power and Meier identify 53 in all, and 28 at the peak, in mid-1857. They note that Groce's figure matches a list by Bell that includes people who never lived on the island.

## What This Changes

The article doesn't dispute that the community existed: it moves its origin, shrinks its numbers, and separates the history of a gene from that of a language. A simple story (English settlers, hereditary deafness, 133 years of signing) comes apart into two dates and two populations that had to be counted one by one. Barely 40 years separate the birth of Benjamin Mayhew from the arrival of three young girls at Hartford: what played out in that span remains an open question.

repere.texte: Power and Meier (2024) date the birth of the Chilmark signing community to February 1785, not 1692: about 40 years of independent development, not 133, before three young deaf women arrived in 1825 at the American School for the Deaf in Hartford.
repere.source: Power, J. M. & Meier, R. P., “The Historical Demography of the Martha's Vineyard Signing Community,” Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education, 29(3), 2024, pp. 295-321

carte.punch: “The whole island signed, going back to English settlers”: a 2024 study cuts 133 years to 40.
carte.idee: Nora Ellen Groce traced Martha's Vineyard sign language back to 1692 and to English settlers, or 133 years of independent development. A 2024 study (Power and Meier) has it born in Chilmark in February 1785, for some 40 years before 1825.
carte.source_courte: Power & Meier, J. of Deaf Studies, 2024

quiz.question: According to the Power and Meier study (2024), what changes from Nora Ellen Groce's account of the Martha's Vineyard signing community?
choix: The community never existed: it would be a local legend with no demographic basis
The origin would be later (1785, not 1692) and the period of independent development shorter (about 40 years, not 133)
Sign language would have arrived directly from England with no transformation on the island
The total number of deaf people counted would have stayed strictly identical between the two studies
quiz.explication: Power and Meier place the origin of the signing community in February 1785, with the birth of Benjamin Mayhew, not in 1692; the period of independent development before the encounter with Hartford in 1825 thus falls to about 40 years. The community's existence isn't called into question, the language doesn't come directly from Kent (the signing community is new, with no link to Kent's signing communities), and the counts of deaf people differ between the two studies (72 versus 53 in total).

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Nora Ellen Groce's classic account (1985) propose about the origin of the signing community?
choix: An origin in 1692, with settlers from Kent carrying a recessive gene for deafness
An origin in the 20th century, imported by the Hartford school
An unknown origin, Groce refusing to date the phenomenon
An origin tied to settlers from Scotland in the 18th century
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Groce tied the signing community to settlers from Kent, England, carrying a recessive gene for deafness, with an origin of 1692, or 133 years of independent development.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many deaf people do Power and Meier identify on the island between 1692 and 1998, and at what peak?
choix: 72 in all, with a peak of 45 in the 1840s
53 in all, with a peak of 28 in mid-1857
11 in all, all grouped in Chilmark
93 in all, with a peak of 133 in 1825
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Power and Meier identify 53 deaf people between 1692 and 1998, with a peak of 28 in mid-1857, figures lower than Groce's, 72 in all and a peak of 45 in the 1840s.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens on October 25, 1825, in Power and Meier's account?
choix: The birth of Benjamin Mayhew, the first deaf person in Chilmark
The publication of Nora Ellen Groce's book
Three young deaf women from the island enter the American School for the Deaf in Hartford
The closing of the Chilmark school by the Massachusetts authorities
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On October 25, 1825, Lovey Mayhew, Sally Smith, and Mary Smith enter the American School for the Deaf in Hartford, which had opened eight years earlier, marking the end of the period of independent development described by Power and Meier.
